Cash is $247. I own three red properties with one house each, plus two mortgaged ones. p2 has full pinks with no houses. p3 owns Baltic, Oriental, and several utilities. p4 has railroads and utilities.

I missed buying Oriental Avenue. p3 won it at auction for $120. Building another house on each red property would cost $450. That exceeds my cash. I will likely unmortgage the two reds or trade.

Only one house can be built on a red property. That costs $150 and leaves $97. Two houses would cost $300 and leave a deficit.

Building one more house would leave only $97. That is too little to survive a Chairman of the Board fine, repairs, or income tax. The previous strategy was to keep a large cash buffer. Two houses on one red property would raise rent sharply, but that risk is too dangerous with such a thin reserve.

One house on Illinois would raise rent from $100 to $300. That is the highest traffic property. The $150 cost is justified by the expected value. p2 has full pink monopoly and $963. They will likely build heavily there soon. Landing on pinks could wipe me out.

p2 is next. They are on Virginia Avenue and could build houses before anyone lands on my reds. I am now considering trade offers to strengthen my position.

I am evaluating specific trade offers. p3 lacks a full orange monopoly because Tennessee is still on the bank. Trading New York Avenue to p3 would help them complete that set, but they would still need Tennessee from the bank. That makes the trade risky if someone else buys Tennessee. I previously offered p4 Vermont Avenue for $150, but they refused.

Selling Vermont Avenue would raise cash to fund house building. Either p3 or p4 could then complete a light blue set, but neither would immediately own a full monopoly. Unmortgaging the two red properties costs $55 and $110 respectively. That is too expensive for the small rent gain without a full set.

Unmortgaging New York Avenue would yield only $16 in base rent, so that is a waste of cash. I am now calculating the exact risk of building one more house on Illinois. A Chairman of the Board fine costs $150, which exceeds the remaining $97. Selling one house for $75 would cover the fine and leave $22. Repairs for four houses cost $100, which also exceeds the balance; selling one house for $75 covers repairs and leaves $97.

I am now weighing whether to build one more house on Illinois. Selling houses to cover a $200 income tax would leave me with two houses and only $47 cash, which is messy and uneven. The probability of drawing bad cards versus landing on Illinois is uncertain. I am reconsidering the earlier strategy of keeping a large cash buffer, since p2 has a full pink monopoly and will likely build heavily soon. I may need to race ahead or propose a trade to raise cash.

p2 has no immediate need for any of my properties. p3 could buy mortgaged New York Avenue for $150 to $200, but they still need Tennessee from the bank to complete their orange set, so it is not an urgent trade.

I am now considering a trade for mortgaged Vermont Avenue. p3 just paid $120 for Oriental Avenue, so they might pay for Vermont to complete a light blue set. p4 has Connecticut and $915 in cash. A trade war between them could raise my cash by over $200. I can only take one action this turn, but proposing a trade might still give me another decision if it is rejected.

Proposing a trade consumes this turn but may grant another post-turn action afterward. I am weighing whether to trade for cash before building, or to build now since I already hold the only developed monopoly.

p2 has undeveloped pink properties and $963. They will likely build three houses immediately on their turn. Three houses on pinks pay over $700. I need both a cash cushion and higher rents. One house each leaves me too fragile. Building Illinois to two houses would raise rent to $300. That is meaningful against p2's $963. The cost leaves me vulnerable. I am now leaning toward building Illinois to two houses.

The Chairman of the Board fine is a fixed $150, not multiplied by the number of houses. That makes it manageable with one house on Illinois, since selling it for $75 would cover the cost. Repairs still cost $100 for four houses, which remains a risk. I am now checking whether Community Chest cards include a Chairman event.

The Chairman of the Board is a Chance card, not a Community Chest event. With $247, I can afford both the $150 fine and the $100 repairs without selling a house. Building one more house on Illinois would force me to sell it for $75 just to survive those same cards, wasting the development effort.

Neither p3 nor p4 can complete a full light blue monopoly from this trade alone, so the property has limited strategic value. I am now considering asking $150 cash for it, since p3 has $1067 and previously overpaid for Oriental Avenue.

A $150 cash offer for mortgaged Vermont Avenue would raise my total to $397. That is enough to build one house and keep the same $247 buffer, or build two houses and leave only $97. The trade is worth trying even if rejected, since I can still build or end my turn. I am now deciding which opponent to offer it to.

I am now weighing specific cash offers for mortgaged Vermont Avenue. p3 has $1067 and recently overpaid for Oriental Avenue, so they may be willing to pay $200 for the property even though it does not complete their light blue set. p4 previously refused a $150 offer and is aware that holding Vermont prevents p3 from completing two-thirds of the light blue group, so they might accept a higher bid around $175 to block that progression.

I will propose the trade to p3. They have the most cash and recently invested in Oriental Avenue, so they are the strongest bidder. I can also tell p4 that p3 is offering for Vermont to pressure them into outbidding.

I will ask $200 cash for mortgaged Vermont Avenue. If p3 refuses, I can lower the offer or try p4 next. I will not sell New York Avenue to p3, since they could immediately complete their orange set by buying Tennessee from the bank.

I am now leaning toward building one house on Illinois. Indiana and Kentucky would raise rent by $160, but Illinois offers the largest jump to $300. It is also landed on most frequently because of jail exits and Chance cards. I will not trade with p2 or buy railroads.

I am now weighing the trade-off of building one more house on Illinois. A $150 cost leaves only $97 cash, but that is safer than the $7 buffer I previously deemed fatal. If a bad card hits, I can sell the house for $75 and survive. If not, I face a $300 rent trap on the best property. p2 is currently at Virginia.

I mapped the board positions. p2 is at Virginia (space 14). p4 is on Indiana (space 23). p3 is at New York Avenue (space 19).

p2 at Virginia can land on my red properties with rolls of 7 through 10. p3 at New York Avenue is only two spaces away from Kentucky, Indiana, and Illinois, so they can also hit reds easily.

The expected rent increase from one house on Illinois is roughly $40 this round. The downside risk is smaller than previously feared because bad cards are rare and only trigger when landed on. With $247 in cash, a $97 buffer survives most events. Selling the house would cover the Chairman fine, repairs, or a $200 tax without bankruptcy. Building one house on Illinois is now the chosen action.

I will build one house on Illinois Avenue. I cannot afford to develop all three red properties at once. The public message will stay strategic and avoid revealing my cash shortage. I also noted that p2 will likely build houses on their pink properties next.

p2 has $963 and could build three houses on their pink properties, leaving only $63. That would generate $700 to $750 in rent per landing. One extra house on Illinois is not enough to survive that. I am now considering the trade for cash as a better way to fund two or three houses on the reds.

Two houses on the reds would cost $450, leaving a $3 deficit. That is too tight. I will build one house on Illinois instead. The engine may pause for a trade rejection and return to me, so I can still build before ending my turn.

I am now questioning whether proposing a trade actually ends my post-turn sequence. The engine may pause for the other player's response, which would return to me and allow me to build before ending my turn.

Proposing a trade should not block the house build, since the engine returns to me after the other player responds. A cash offer for mortgaged Vermont Avenue is now being evaluated; p3 may pay $80 to $120 for it.

A $100 offer for mortgaged Vermont Avenue would leave $347 cash, enough for one house with a $197 buffer. That is safer than the $97 buffer from a $150 house build. p4 may now accept a $150 bid because blocking p3 from completing their light blue set has increased in value.

I will propose mortgaged Vermont Avenue to p4 for $160 cash. This blocks p3 from completing their light blue set before they can buy it. I am also considering a lower offer to p3, around $140, since they may accept a simpler deal.

p3 has $1067 in cash, so a $140 offer is easily affordable. Selling mortgaged Vermont Avenue to p4 would leave p3 with only one light blue property and block them from completing the set. p4 would not gain a color monopoly, since they already own railroads, so this trade is less dangerous than letting p3 acquire the property.

I will ask $175 cash from p4 for mortgaged Vermont Avenue. If that offer is rejected, I will try p3 next.

I will not offer p4 cash for mortgaged Vermont Avenue. They are organizing a cash boycott and explicitly refuse to fund red house development.

I will build one house on Illinois Avenue. The cash boycott rules out any trade, so I cannot wait for a better offer. I will keep the public message short and confident while hiding my cash stress.

I will not unmortgage Vermont Avenue. Selling the house back for $75 would survive a fine or tax, so that risk is manageable. I cannot trade New York Avenue to p2 or p4 either; p2 would only buy it as an investment or blocker, and p4 still boycotts cash. I will build one house on Illinois and end my turn.

messages.content:
You are an autonomous player in a game of Monopoly competing against other AI players.

Your goal is to win the game by maximizing long-term advantage and being the last non-bankrupt player. You may use any legal strategy or personality (aggressive, deceptive, cooperative, conservative, manipulative, opportunistic, friendly, hostile, etc.) and may adapt dynamically as the game evolves.

You will receive the following inputs:

1) System Prompt (this message): authoritative instructions.
2) Game State: full board/game context + memory (public chat, recent actions, your private thoughts).
3) Action State: exact dynamic context for the current decision and legal action schemas.

### Action Rules
- Make exactly one tool call per decision.
- Use only tools listed as legal for that decision.
- Never invent tools, arguments, or targets.
- Obey the provided argument schema exactly.
- If a tool requires no arguments, pass none.

### Messages
Each action must include both fields:
- Public Message: visible to other players. Use it to negotiate, bluff, deceive, cooperate, intimidate, joke, or stay silent — whatever best serves your strategy.
- Private Thoughts: visible only to you. Use it to reason honestly, track strategy, analyze opponents, and leave notes for your future self. Be concise but clear.
- Keep both messages token-efficient and concise.

### Strategy Guidance
- Play strategically with long-term outcomes in mind.
- Observe opponents and adapt.
- Deception in public chat is allowed; private thoughts should reflect true reasoning.
- Be consistent unless there is a reason to change.
- Prefer concise reasoning and communication.

Your role is not to explain rules or debug the system.  
Your role is to **play Monopoly and win**.

When a decision is presented, think carefully and make one legal tool call that best advances your chances of winning.
